title: A Law Is Only Real When a Machine Enforces It

intelligence.essence: Written law is tuition; operating law is a machine that can say NO. Candidate bytes may be validated, compiled, tested, and explained — but they may never govern until the director's exact-version ratification, a receipt, and the full gate set are all in place. Authorization binds to an (action, SHA, moment) triple. A policy cannot self-extend, and the machine-readable artifact governs over prose minimums. Ratifying the law does not freeze the document. A rule nobody can fail at is not a law — encode it as a mandatory step in the path every seat must walk. A fail-closed repair ships with its provisioning, sequenced. Four links, and the law is not real until all four hold: write it, wire it, prove it, cite it.
intelligence.human_view: The Scorecard Law's enforcement tool was fully written and correct — 371 lines, its own docstring saying "the receipt IS the Scorecard Law's five steps" — and nothing in CI invoked it. Zero workflow hits. A law with an enforcement tool that nothing invokes is a wish, not a law. The positive control proves the pattern works: the deletion-discipline law went from ratified text to a guard wired as a required CI check, with 33 of 33 tests green and error text citing the note — a deletion that violates the law now fails CI. That chain has four links: WRITE the enforcement tool, WIRE it (a CI workflow actually invokes it, required), PROVE it (a red test or observed CI failure shows the wire is live), CITE it (the tool's errors name the note so the law is findable from the failure). An unwired guard fails at link two. The same night, two more laws got machines behind them — a tip-currency gate that blocks any consequential action on a moved tip, and a capture gate that fails closed on side memory channels — and the director's standing order landed with them: show, don't tell; if we can code it, we code it; make it machine law, machine-forced.
intelligence.child_view: Imagine a rule on the classroom wall that says "no running in the hall." If nobody ever stops a runner, the rule is just words on a wall. Now imagine a gate across the hall that only opens when you walk. That gate is the rule, working. Writing the rule is the easy part. Building the gate is the job.
intelligence.grandma_view: A rule nobody enforces is a wish, not a rule. If you want people to do the right thing, do not just write it down — build it into the way the work happens, so the wrong thing cannot happen quietly. And when you write a new rule, check that the machine that enforces it is actually switched on.
intelligence.ai_view: For every doctrine, ask one question: does a machine enforce it? If the answer is no, the next action is to code the machine — not to write a better note about it. When you design a gate, authenticate its own terms from its own canonical record — never trust caller-supplied claims about expiry or scope — and make protected paths structurally unpromotable without a human. When you propose a fail-closed gate, ship the provisioning with it: merge lands, grant is issued, and until the grant exists the system correctly refuses — and park that sequenced plan with the gate owner instead of silently owning a production write. Never let a single flag activate a candidate: flipping the runtime flag alone is tested and refused. And keep the law and the document on separate lifecycles — ratification blesses the enforcement point, not the prose, which keeps being scorecarded toward ten.
intelligence.what_it_means: There are two layers to every law — the written word and the machine that can say NO — and a ratified law without a machine is an aspiration. The activation ladder exists so a candidate can never promote itself from "validated idea" to "governing law," and the four-link chain exists so a written enforcement tool can never be mistaken for an enforced law. Together they are the difference between a system governed by text and a system governed by behavior.
whats_inside: Show, don't tell. If we can code it, we code it — write it, wire it, prove it, cite it.
There are two layers to every law — the written word and the machine that can say NO — and a ratified law without a machine is an aspiration.

The team wrote beautiful laws and then watched the same failures recur — decisions on moved tips, promotions on self-asserted names, merges that skipped the gate — because the lesson was written and nothing enforced it.
WRITE — the enforcement tool exists and encodes the ratified law
WIRE — a CI workflow invokes it, required; grep the invokers, never just the tree — presence is not enforcement, invocation is
PROVE — a red test or an observed CI failure shows the wire is live, plus a falsifier battery

CITE — the tool's errors name the SN. Activation conjunction for any candidate law: exact-version human ratification AND receipt AND status RATIFIED_ACTIVE AND ratified=true AND runtime_enabled=true AND source pins reconciled AND schema / nine-node / hard-stop / truth-distinction gates PASS.
